learningObjectives.title: Challenges to Elizabeth at home and abroad
Elizabethan society in the Age of Exploration

questions.q: In which year did Elizabeth I become Queen of England?
questions.explain: Elizabeth succeeded her half-sister Mary I in 1558.

questions.q: Who served as Elizabeth's Secretary of State and most trusted advisor from 1558?
options: Sir William Cecil
Sir Francis Drake
Robert Dudley
Sir Walter Raleigh
questions.explain: William Cecil (later Lord Burghley) was Elizabeth's leading advisor and Secretary of State.

questions.q: Why did the 1559 Religious Settlement make Elizabeth 'Supreme Governor' of the Church rather than 'Supreme Head'?
options: To make the title more acceptable to Catholics and those who objected to a woman heading the Church
Because the Pope kept the title of Supreme Head
Because Parliament had abolished the monarchy's religious role
Because she had not yet been crowned
questions.explain: 'Supreme Governor' was a compromise title that offended fewer Catholics and critics than 'Supreme Head'.

questions.q: What did the 1559 Act of Uniformity establish?
options: A single Book of Common Prayer to be used in all churches
The Pope as head of the English Church
Compulsory Latin Mass in every parish
The abolition of Parliament
questions.explain: The Act of Uniformity set out one Book of Common Prayer and the appearance of churches and services.

questions.q: Why is Elizabeth's Religious Settlement often described as a 'middle way' (via media)?
options: It tried to satisfy both Catholics and Protestants and avoid extremes
It banned all forms of worship
It made England fully Catholic again
It handed control of the Church to the Puritans
questions.explain: The Settlement sought a moderate compromise acceptable to as many people as possible.

questions.q: A Catholic gentry family quietly refuses to attend Church of England services. What term describes them, and what penalty could they face?
options: Recusants, who could be fined one shilling a week
Puritans, who were imprisoned for life
Separatists, who were exiled abroad
Vagabonds, who were whipped
questions.explain: Catholics who refused to attend services were recusants, fined a shilling per week under the Act of Uniformity.

questions.q: In which year did the Revolt of the Northern Earls take place?
questions.explain: The Northern Earls, led by Northumberland and Westmorland, rebelled in 1569.

questions.q: What was a central aim of the Revolt of the Northern Earls in 1569?
options: To replace Elizabeth with Mary, Queen of Scots and restore Catholicism
To make England a Puritan republic
To crown Philip II of Spain as king
To abolish Parliament permanently
questions.explain: The earls planned to depose Elizabeth, put the Catholic Mary on the throne and marry her to the Duke of Norfolk.

questions.q: Why was Pope Pius V's 1570 Papal Bull dangerous for English Catholics?
options: By excommunicating Elizabeth it encouraged Catholics to overthrow her, making loyalty and treason harder to separate
It ordered all Catholics to leave England at once
It forced Catholics to convert to Protestantism
It made Catholicism the official religion of England
questions.explain: The Bull 'Regnans in Excelsis' released Catholics from obedience to Elizabeth, so Catholics were increasingly viewed with suspicion.

questions.q: Why was the Duke of Norfolk executed in 1572?
options: For his involvement in the Ridolfi Plot to overthrow Elizabeth
For leading the Spanish Armada
For refusing to attend church
For helping Drake raid Spanish ships
questions.explain: Norfolk was implicated in Roberto Ridolfi's 1571 plot to depose Elizabeth and marry Mary, Queen of Scots.

questions.q: The Babington Plot of 1586 directly led to which event?
options: The execution of Mary, Queen of Scots
The launch of the Spanish Armada
The Revolt of the Northern Earls
The signing of the Religious Settlement
questions.explain: Evidence from the Babington Plot implicated Mary and led to her execution in 1587.

questions.q: Who was Elizabeth's 'spymaster', responsible for uncovering several Catholic plots?
options: Sir Francis Walsingham
Sir William Cecil
Robert Dudley
Sir Francis Drake
questions.explain: Walsingham ran an extensive spy network that exposed plots such as the Throckmorton and Babington plots.

questions.q: Which factor most contributed to Philip II of Spain launching the Armada in 1588?
options: English support for Dutch Protestant rebels and Drake's raids on Spanish ships
An English invasion of mainland Spain
A trade treaty signed with the Pope
The death of Philip's first wife
questions.explain: Religious rivalry, aid to the Dutch (Treaty of Nonsuch) and privateering all pushed Philip towards invasion.

questions.q: Who commanded the Spanish Armada in 1588?
options: The Duke of Medina Sidonia
The Duke of Parma
The Duke of Norfolk
King Philip II himself
questions.explain: Medina Sidonia led the Armada after the death of the more experienced Marquis of Santa Cruz.

questions.q: Why were the English fireships at Calais so effective against the Armada?
options: They forced the Spanish ships to cut anchor and break their tight formation
They sank the entire Spanish fleet
They carried the English army onto Spanish decks
They blockaded the coast of Spain
questions.explain: Fear of fireships scattered the crescent formation, leaving Spanish ships vulnerable at Gravelines.

questions.q: A source notes that English ships at Gravelines were smaller, faster and more manoeuvrable than the Spanish galleons. This best helps explain why the English could...
options: Outmanoeuvre the Spanish and fire on them more effectively
Lose the battle quickly and retreat
Ignore the weather entirely
Board and capture every Spanish ship
questions.explain: Faster, lighter English ships could keep their distance and use their guns while avoiding Spanish boarding tactics.

questions.q: Which English sailor completed a circumnavigation of the globe between 1577 and 1580?
options: Sir Francis Drake
Sir Walter Raleigh
John Hawkins
Sir Humphrey Gilbert
questions.explain: Drake circumnavigated the world in the Golden Hind, returning laden with Spanish treasure.

questions.q: In the Elizabethan social hierarchy (the 'Great Chain of Being'), which group ranked highest below the monarch?
options: The nobility
Yeomen
Tenant farmers
Vagrants
questions.explain: Below the monarch came the nobility, then the gentry, and so on down the ordered social hierarchy.

questions.q: A fit, healthy man with no work wanders from town to town begging. How would Elizabethan authorities most likely classify and treat him?
options: As a 'sturdy beggar' or vagabond, who could be whipped or punished
As deserving poor, given generous relief
As a yeoman, granted land
As gentry, excused from work
questions.explain: The able-bodied poor were seen as idle 'sturdy beggars' and faced harsh punishment rather than sympathy.

questions.q: A merchant explains the growth of English exploration in the 1570s and 1580s. Which factor best supports his argument?
options: Improvements in ship design and navigation, together with the promise of new trade and wealth
A sharp decline in demand for foreign goods
A royal ban on long sea voyages
England being at peace with every European power
questions.explain: Better galleons and instruments like the astrolabe, plus the lure of trade and riches, drove Elizabethan exploration.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE History (1HI0) specification; Early Elizabethan England 1558-88
